entry.title: Brown graduate students: Your research matters. Now's your chance to share it!

media:group.media:title: Brown graduate students: Your research matters. Now's your chance to share it!
media:group.media:description:
Applications are open for Research Matters, an annual event hosted by Brown's Graduate School that gives master's and Ph.D. students the opportunity to share their research through short, engaging talks designed for a general audience.
For a glimpse of what Research Matters is all about, meet Heather Valeria, a Brown Ph.D. candidate who took the stage at last year's event to share her research exploring how female reproductive organs can influence brain health and overall well-being.
Now it's your turn! All Brown master's and Ph.D. students are encouraged to apply for the next Research Matters event, taking place in April 2027: go.brown.edu/researchmatters

entry.title: Human Life is Sacred, Art is not: a conversation with Samar Haddad King

media:group.media:title: Human Life is Sacred, Art is not: a conversation with Samar Haddad King
media:group.media:description:
Artist Samar Haddad King in conversation with Nadje Al-Ali, Nancy Duke Lewis Professor of Anthropology and Gender Studies, Professor of Anthropology and Gender and Sexuality Studies, Brown University, and Kathryn Spellman Poots, Academic Director, Middle East Institute, Columbia University How does war live in the body, and what can dance register that testimony cannot? The Gender, Art and Body Politics series continues with Samar Haddad King, choreographer, composer and founding artistic director of Yaa Samar! Dance Theatre, which has worked between New York and Palestine since 2011. Her recent pieces include Losing It, co-created with Samaa Wakim, Last Ward and Gathering. In conversation with Nadje Al-Ali and Kathryn Spellman Poots, King will discuss the gendered body as an archive of political violence, working across borders and checkpoints, and making Palestinian art in a time of genocide.
November 2, 2026 Brown University

entry.title: AASLH & NCPH Simmons Center Workshop | Grad Student Summer Practicums in the Public Humanities

media:group.media:title: AASLH & NCPH Simmons Center Workshop | Grad Student Summer Practicums in the Public Humanities
media:group.media:description:
From September 16 through 19, 2026, the AASLH & NCPH Joint Conference (American Association for State and Local History and the National Council on Public History) took place in Providence, RI. On September 16, the Simmons Center hosted a full-day workshop entitled “Public History at the Ruth J. Simmons Center for the Study of Slavery and Justice.”
In this session, six second-year A.M. Public Humanities students gave lightning round presentations about their summer practicum experiences moderated by Prof. Elena Shih, Director of Graduate Studies, MA in Public Humanities and Associate Director of Academics at the Ruth J. Simmons Center for the Study of Slavery & Justice. The students’ practicum experiences were hosted by the RISD Museum, Primus House/Center for Reconciliation, the Tomaquag Museum, Printed Matter (NYC), the International Slavery Museum in Liverpool, and Tate Liverpool. Their presentations revolved around the community-oriented and decolonial approaches to museums, archives, curation, public programming, and moving from academic to public practice. This conference workshop was attended by public history professionals from sites such as the National Trust for Historic Preservation, The Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of American History, National Geographic Society, Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History, Hobart and William Smith Colleges, South Carolina State Museum, University of Virginia, University of Michigan, as well as many other institutions of higher education and cultural heritage institutions.
Presenting Students:
Tara Leininger was a special projects intern at Primus House/Center for Reconciliation, where she developed a program proposal for the 2027 Black press bicentennial. Her research explores how museums and cultural institutions can responsibly navigate power and community relationships. She also serves as a student ambassador for the program.
Caleigh Lyons was an archival intern at the Tomaquag Museum in Exeter, Rhode Island. Her research explores indigeneity and queerness in activating the archive, and she is currently gathering trans and non-binary oral histories of Rhode Island with the Queer Stories Project.
Ivie Orobaton completed a practicum in the contemporary art department at the RISD Museum. They made their curatorial debut with Port Cities and Our Present: Sites of Remaking, on view at the Simmons Center Gallery, and hope to pursue a Ph.D. in history.
Jovanna Walker completed her practicum at the International Slavery Museum in Liverpool. Her research explores museums as venues for freedom dreaming and collective liberation, and she co-directs the Simmons Center's carceral studies reading group.
Alijah Webb completed her practicum at the International Slavery Museum and Tate Liverpool. She was Program Associate at the Foundation for Contemporary Arts, co-founded Perennial Mag, and leads craft workshops in Providence through Cutest Craft Club.
Jun Ying Wen held a joint bibliographic and programming role at Printed Matter, an artist bookstore and nonprofit. Her research looks at print and publishing as sites of knowledge production from the margins.
Chapters: 0:00 - Introduction 1:28 - Tara Leninger 7:00 - Caleigh Lyons 12:57 - Ivie Orobaton 18:36 - Jovanna Walker 26:16 - Alijah Webb 32:03 - Jun Ying Wen 37:20 - Student Q&A

media:group.media:title: 2026 Brown University Opening Convocation
media:group.media:description:
Brown University President Christina H. Paxson will officially proclaim the opening of the 2026-27 academic year and welcome new students to campus at Brown’s 263rd Opening Convocation. Prior to the ceremony, new incoming students will take part in a procession through the Van Wickle Gates — a tradition marking the beginning of their Brown education and their entrance into the Brown community. Traditionally, students pass through the open gates only once more during their time at Brown, exiting outward at Commencement. The 2026 keynote address “Why Openness and a Willingness to Take Risks Will Drive Your Success at Brown and Beyond” will be delivered by James R. Kellner, professor of ecology, evolution and organismal biology, professor of environment and society, and Associate Provost for Corporate Engagement at Brown University.
September 8, 2026 Brown University
